title: 7.2 · Build day
name: Build day
summary: Build day for teams of three: approved teams send the sheet's message, run the five-row test table against the game, find the input that breaks it and send one precise fix. The others build on paper first (three storyboard panels and the test table) and the halves swap. No warm-up: the build queue needs the minutes. The plan page's Builder status line says the morning of whether the Builder is on or resting.
iCan: write test cases before I test, including an edge case
find the input that breaks my game and describe it exactly
ask for one precise fix at a time
materials: Builder etiquette card printable (one per team, stays on the desk)
storyboard sheet with three panels and the five-row test table (one per team)
the team folders with the approved planning sheets and the captains' login cards
the plan page open on the Builder status line
doNow: Write two test cases for your game: the input, and what should happen. Make one of them an edge: the last second, zero lives, an empty answer.
plan: Arrive, captains log in, Do Now
Explore: the etiquette card, the Builder status line, one row of a test table
Rotation 1: approved teams build (message, test table, one fix); the others build on paper

do: Put the etiquette card on the projector and read it; point at the printed one on every desk. Show the Builder status line on the plan page and name the rotation 1 teams.
With the class, fill one row of a test table for the frog quiz on the board: input, a wrong answer; expected, the score stays the same; actual, blank until tested; pass, blank.
say: Write the test cases first, then test. If you only test what you happen to notice, you miss the edges: the last second of the timer, zero lives, the tenth question.
A precise fix names the input, what you expected and what happened: Expected the score to stay the same when a life is lost; it goes up by one. One change per message.
ask: Which three inputs would you test on a timer, and why those three?
explore.afterAsk: Start, halfway and the last second: write them on the board as the model range. Every team's table needs one edge row.
explore.bigIdea: Test cases first, the breaking input named, one precise fix: that is how a game gets built.

play.prefill: the team's Builder message from the planning sheet, pasted first into the build step body (the first 300 characters open the Studio message box)
play.shape: one good message, then one fix; paper prototyping first for the teams not yet approved
rotations: Rotation 1 (15 minutes): approved teams press Start building. The captain sends the sheet's message; the tester runs the five-row test table against the game and fills actual and pass for each row; the team picks the failing row that matters most and sends one precise fix. The other teams build on paper: three storyboard panels and their own test table, then play-test a neighbor team's paper prototype row by row.
Rotation 2 (15 minutes): swap. Paper teams whose sheet is approved press Start building; the teams that built go to paper and run their table against a neighbor team's prototype.

play.builderStatus: on the plan page the morning of: Builder: on / resting, and about how many teams can build this period; resting means the whole class takes the paper path and build day moves to the next period
lookFors: a test table with no edge row: ask for the last second, zero lives or an empty answer
a fix message that says broken or make it harder: send them back to the row: input, expected, actual

play.misconception: Students think testing means playing the game until something looks wrong; a test table decides what to check before you play, so the edges get checked too and the fix message can name the input.
earlyFinishers: a variable the player can see: ask for a score or a timer, then add two rows to the table for it and run them
run your table against a neighbor team's game and hand them the failing row

discuss: Which row of the test table failed first, and what exactly did your fix message say?

rubric.line: Systematic testing: test cases first, the breaking input named, one precise fix
levels: Names the input, the expected and actual result, and the fix message that changed it
Also covers an edge case, or reports a second run of the table after the fix

support: start from the Quiz Show template as it is: a team with a weak plan sends one message that changes only the questions, then tests three rows
the test table comes with the first two rows filled in (a right answer, a wrong answer); the team adds the edge rows
the message starter on the card: Input ___. Expected ___. Actual ___. Please ___.
stretch: a variable the player can see and two table rows that check it, including its edge (zero, the maximum)
a second fix that comes from a neighbor team's run of your table, not from your own

unpluggedTwin.title: Paper prototype play-test
steps: Teams draw the three screens of their game on the storyboard panels: what the player sees first, playing, winning or losing, with the variables shown on each screen.
A neighbor team runs its own five-row test table against the paper prototype: the maker turns the panels, the tester names the input, the note-taker writes actual and pass for each row.
Makers fix one panel because of the failing row that matters most and say what they changed.
Swap roles and test the other team's prototype.

subPlan: Do Now on paper, 3 minutes: two test cases for your game, the input and what should happen; one of them an edge (the last second, zero lives, an empty answer).

Paper prototype day for everyone: teams draw the three screens of their game on the storyboard sheet, a neighbor team runs the five-row test table against it (input, expected, actual, pass?), makers fix one panel because of the failing row that matters most, then the teams swap. No Builder today and no login needed.
Paper exit ticket: the half-sheet with three questions and the sentence frame. Collect it with the test tables.

table: Explore: the etiquette card and one table row

shortPeriod40.keep: the exit ticket is never cut; the five minutes come out of the two build rotations

add: a third rotation so every team gets a second fix and a second run of the table
the full paper prototype play-test for every team before anyone builds
10 minutes of the Unit 7 review on Brain Board

notes: No warm-up today on purpose: the build queue needs the minutes, and the playtest lesson's warm-up covers today's items.
Builder status: check the plan page the morning of. Resting means the whole class takes the paper path and build day moves to the next period; the paper lesson still counts.

Captains only: one game per account per build step, so the captain signs in and presses Start building; the other teammates have no build cell. Mark them with Also mark these teammates when you mark the Program line.

Before this period, paste each team's message from the third question step of Plan your game into the top of this lesson's Build your game step in your copy, or hand the team its sheet and let the captain paste the message into the Studio box.
Ten messages for the whole project per team, and one or two build turns per team per period, are realistic: one good message, the table, one fix is the whole of today.

The Program line of the rubric is builds-toward only (named variables, loops and conditions are the Builder's work): mark it, but it counts as evidence for nothing on the Standards tab. Systematic testing is the line this lesson evidences, through the sentence step.
Discuss is one minute by construction; the one prompt is enough.

steps.title: Today
steps.body:
Do Now: Write two test cases for your game: the input, and what should happen. Make one of them an edge: the last second, zero lives, an empty answer.

Big idea: Test cases first, the breaking input named, one precise fix: that is how a game gets built.

Today half the teams build and half build on paper, then you swap. Your captain signs in.

We will talk about:
- Which row of the test table failed first, and what exactly did your fix message say?

steps.title: Builder etiquette
steps.body:
Keep this card on your desk.
- One change per message.
- Say what you saw and what you expected: Input ___. Expected ___. Actual ___. Please ___.
- Play your game after every change, and run your test table.
- Ten messages for the whole project. Make each one count.
- Never put your full name, your school or anyone else's name in a message or in the game. First names or avatars only, and only in the credits.
- If the Builder is resting, switch to the paper prototype.
- Demos show the game, not the chat.

steps.title: Build your game

levels: Attempted: the game runs; nothing the player can see changes
Meets: a visible variable (score, lives or time) and a condition or a loop the player can see
Exceeds: the team can point to where the variable changes and where the condition or loop runs

steps.body:
Paste your team's Builder message here (up to 300 characters).

Then:
- Press Start building when your teacher has approved your sheet.
- Send the message. While it builds, write expected into every row of your test table.
- Play the game and run the table: fill actual and pass for each row. Include the edge row.
- Pick the failing row that matters most. Send one fix message: input, expected, actual. Run the table again.
- Hand in when your teacher says so.

The card: one change per message; say what you saw and what you expected; play after every change; no full names anywhere; if the Builder is resting, build on paper; demos show the game, not the chat.

steps.title: Exit ticket
steps.body: Three quick questions about test cases and precise fixes.

steps.title: In your own words
steps.body:
Which input broke your game, what did you expect and what happened, and what did your fix message change?
